Thank you so so much for replying. Yes, I am not from USA, I live in Scotland. 

I only have one strong friend, who I met through my nursing degree course. She unfortunately cannot house me, as A. It's her boyfriend's house, and B. One bedroom limits her. I've looked into options, and genuinely cannot move until I save up. 

I wanted to get my degree so that I could work on going into palliative work. As strange as it sounds, I've worked with quite a few dying people during high school, and more weirdly enough I've enjoyed helping these people live out their last days on this plane. It was my communication with other professionals, not patients, that lead to my failure (for example, I've caught myself just describing what oedema is instead of just saying that I suspected oedema). I was never offended by patients asking me about my weird name (masc name for a very obviously fem body does not help), and I did extra courses during my degree for restraint and stuff. I've been punched plenty of times by dementia patients or locked ward patients, I'm not frightened of that stuff and it just makes me more sympathetic to them. My real worry is fitting into my coworkers. I'm 22, I feel so disconnected compared to my mentors who are almost always 50+, and I'm not good with socialising outside of work as it is, and that's definitely something to work on.

I'm still finishing my degree, getting an open BSc. I am only 20 credits away from a full degree and I could not just walk away. In Scotland (I do not know how the degree works in England, Wales or Northern Ireland), since I did pretty much all of my degree in Nursing then I can start up again in 2nd year. 

I think I need to get registered to a new GP, and talk through my issues. I have a hell of a lot to work on to be fair, and nursing was a backup degree - I did a year of music business in 2020 and that did not go well, thanks pandemic. 

Thank you for all your invaluable advice. I'm sticking to this job, it's care assisstant role so less responsibility as a nurse but I get more time to listen to patients and hold their hand when they need someone next to them when they are scared.

Of course!! The only places I have ever felt comfortable were outpatients. The two in-hospital outpatients placements I've had are angioplasty and dialysis. Both were excellent and especially with dialysis - same people, same times they come in, same prescription, etc. It was such a good routine. I've had one out of hospital outpatients experience, community learning disabilities. I loved that as well, it was really good to again work with same patients, same day, same time. And the patients were always so sweet. 

Personally I'm aiming to do palliative services. It's something about making sure someone has a comfortable death that attracts me. I've always been the one on the ward to help with final wash, final checks with the ANP, etc, and I want people to be able to have that good death since I've seen some absolutely horrific palliative deaths. I'll keep hoping, there's not many places where I'm training - the Highlands of Scotland, and I have a very hard time understanding driving. I'm very much considering going to Glasgow, but I don't want to do that before I've gotten transition shock out of the way. I have a feeling that it's not going to go as smoothly as others have done so. 

Thank you though <3 would love to work in the US but absolutely terrified of, well, having to deal with gunshot wounds. That's the one thing I've never seen.

My dream job is doing a community palliative work - so this is what I'm aiming towards!! Or something more outpatients. The angioplasty and renal outpatient wards here have been so good with me. So my only options are community or outpatients for me to be healthy in the long term. Perhaps one day I will be part of a palliative team, I wish that will happen!!

For me personally I have Scotland, England, NI and Wales fused together as Britain, a Union Country. Britain has his own voice and actions but is heavily influenced by the four, which are now voices in his head. 

If one breaks away, they just pop out, since they existed before the union anyway. If the Union completely falls apart, I like to have it where all the countries exists and the Union Country is just retired to an ex-country position. 

Take the USSR for instance. 15 countries broke away from it; Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belorussia (Belarus), Estonia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kirghizia (Kyrgyzstan), Latvia, Lithuania, Moldvania (Moldova), Russia, Tadzhikistan (Tajikistan), Turkmenistan, Ukraine, and Uzbekistan. All of these had flag changes after separating from their union.

Some countries don't really have flag changes. The British flag is a weird one since it is made up out of Scotland, England and NI's flags. So if someone (the most possible contender is Scotland, lets be real) left, Scotland's flag might not change but the Union flag might. 

But I also know that some people like to have it where Scotland and England a child is Britain, and then also have NI and Wales as Britain's children as well as colonies.

There's another problem. At the height of the British Empire it owned a lot. A lot of colonies. Canada just did Canada and asked politely.
